newsitem.title: GERMANY: German hopes for less trade friction with U.S..
newsitem.headline: German hopes for less trade friction with U.S..

text.p: A leading German foreign policy spokesman said on Wednesday a new U.S. secretary of state would temper the Clinton administration's unilateralism, especially in trade policies like the Helms-Burton Act.

Karl Lamers, foreign policy spokesman for Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), told German Radio after President Bill Clinton's reelection that the whole European Union opposed the U.S. law punishing foreign firms that trade with Cuba, Iran or Libya.
He also said: "The problems that have to be solved would have been even more difficult to solve under a President Dole."

Asked if he thought a younger U.S. secretary of state would be more open to the EU's objections than Warren Christopher, who is expected to retire soon, Lamers said: "I hope so. It's quite possible. I see a chance for a change in policy here."

The Helms-Burton Act allows lawsuits to be filed in U.S. courts against foreign firms that own or operate properties seized by Cuba from U.S. citizens who were Cuban nationals before the 1959 communist revolution. Similar laws apply for trade with Iran and Libya.

Clinton ordered the sanctions to come into force last July in a move interpreted here as a pitch to Cuban-American voters, but he delayed implementation for six months to appease U.S. allies who threatened retaliation.
"That is a very problematic stand," Lamers said of recent U.S. trade policy. "It is politely called unilateralism but one could describe it differently."
Germany has come in for U.S. criticism for its "critical dialogue" with Teheran, but Lamers said Iran was clearly a regional power which had to be reckoned with.

"There is also the suspicion that the U.S. supports the Taleban in Afghanistan through Pakistan," he said of the Islamic fundamentalist rebels who drove the Afghan government out of Kabul and are now fighting to keep the capital.
"That doesn't fit with the moral position they (the U.S.) take in the case of Iran," he remarked.
Lamers said the United States and EU should put aside their trade differences and focus on more important problems like the planned expansion of NATO into eastern Europe.

"I hope that Clinton and his new foreign minister will find a solution to the problem of NATO, more precisely the problem of Russia, in a way that amounts to an agreement with Russia," he said. "Nobody is helped if the security situation is more tense after a NATO expansion than before."
He stressed that both the U.S. and the Europeans had an interest in seeing a strong European Union.
"America needs a strong partner that does not only carry out orders made in Washington but works for solutions with America in a certain division of labour," he said.
